questions.explanation: Charging by friction occurs when two insulators are rubbed together, transferring electrons and producing opposite charges on the objects.

questions.text: Coulomb’s law states that the magnitude of the electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

options.text: Only for charges of equal magnitude

questions.explanation: Coulomb’s law: F ∝ |q1 q2| / r^2; the force acts along the line joining the charges.

questions.text: Electrical discharge through air can occur when a large potential difference ionizes the air, creating a conductive path.
questions.explanation: Discharge happens when air is ionized by a strong electric field creating a conductive path (spark, ionization).

questions.text: In a series circuit, the current through each resistor is the same.
questions.explanation: In a series circuit the same current flows through all components; voltages add up across components.

questions.text: Where should a voltmeter be connected to measure the potential difference across a resistor?
questions.explanation: Voltmeter has very high resistance and is connected in parallel to the component whose voltage is measured.

questions.text: Two point charges q1=3 μC and q2=-2 μC are separated by r=0.05 m. Using Coulomb’s law, which is the correct magnitude of the electrostatic force (k=9×10^9 N m^2/C^2)?
questions.explanation: F = k|q1 q2|/r^2 = 9e9 × (3e-6 × 2e-6) / (0.05)^2 = 0.054 / 0.0025 = 21.6 N. Direction is attractive since charges have opposite signs.

questions.text: State Ohm’s law and identify what each symbol represents.
questions.answerKey: Ohm's law: V = IR; V is voltage (potential difference), I is current, R is resistance.
questions.explanation: Ohm’s law relates the current through a conductor to the voltage and its resistance.

questions.text: Explain why an ammeter must be connected in series and a voltmeter in parallel in a circuit.
questions.answerKey: An ammeter is placed in series to measure the current through a component without altering the circuit; a voltmeter is placed in parallel to measure potential difference across a component, while drawing minimal current due to its high resistance.
questions.explanation: Connecting ammeter in series ensures it measures the through-path current; voltmeter in parallel across component measures potential difference without significantly changing current.

questions.text: A resistor of 4 Ω is connected to a 12 V source. Calculate the current flowing through the resistor.
questions.explanation: Using Ohm's law I = V/R, I = 12 V / 4 Ω = 3 A.

questions.text: Two resistors 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V source. Calculate the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination and the total current supplied by the source.
Which method of charging involves transfer of charge by touching two objects together?
questions.explanation: Charging by conduction occurs when electrons are transferred through direct contact between objects.

questions.text: What causes the leaves of a gold-leaf electroscope to diverge when a charged rod is brought near but not touching?
questions.explanation: The presence of a nearby charged object induces charges on the leaves; like charges repel causing divergence.

questions.text: If the distance between two identical charges is doubled, what happens to the electrostatic force between them?
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law states F ∝ 1/r^2; doubling r reduces the force to one quarter.

questions.text: Electric field strength at a point is defined as the force experienced by a test charge per unit charge.
questions.explanation: E = F/q for a small test charge q; the field strength is the force per unit charge.

questions.text: In a parallel circuit with resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω connected to the same 12 V supply, which resistor carries the largest current?
questions.explanation: In parallel, current in each branch is I = V/R. The smallest resistance draws the largest current.

questions.text: Charging by friction creates new electric charges; charge is not conserved.
questions.explanation: Charge is transferred between bodies; total charge is conserved.

questions.text: State Coulomb's law and describe how the force changes when either charge or distance changes.
questions.answerKey: F = k |q1 q2| / r^2. The force increases with the product of the charges and decreases with the square of the distance.
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law relates the electrostatic force between two point charges to the product of the charges and the inverse square of their separation.

questions.text: What is the direction of the electric field inside a conductor at electrostatic equilibrium?
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, charges rearrange so that no net electric field exists inside the conductor.

questions.text: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series to a 9 V battery. Find the current in the circuit (show steps and final unit).
questions.explanation: R_total = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω; I = V / R_total = 9 V / 10 Ω = 0.9 A.

questions.text: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V source. Find the equivalent resistance and the total current drawn from the source (show steps and final units).
Which statement correctly describes a magnet?

options.text: A magnet has two poles: North and South.
A magnet loses magnetic properties only when cooled.
All magnets are temporary and lose magnetism easily.

questions.explanation: Magnets inherently have two poles, North and South. Like poles attract and unlike poles repel. Magnets can attract iron or steel, and they can be permanent, temporary, or electromagnets.

questions.text: Which statement about magnetic field lines around a bar magnet is true?

options.text: Field lines form open curves that end at infinity.
Field lines exit the magnet at the North end and enter at the South end.
Field lines only exist outside the magnet.
Field lines are straight lines radiating out from the magnet.

questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines emerge from the North pole of a magnet and curve around to enter the South pole, forming a pattern that represents the magnetic field.

questions.text: Which statement about the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire is true?

options.text: The field strength increases with distance from the wire.
The field is zero at all points around the wire.
The field strength decreases with distance from the wire (roughly as 1/r).
The field exists only on the surface of the wire.

questions.explanation: Around a long straight wire, magnetic field lines form concentric circles and their strength decreases with distance from the wire, roughly as 1/r.

questions.text: A positive charge moves with velocity v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B. The magnetic force on the charge is:

options.text: Perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field

questions.explanation: The magnetic force on a moving charge in a magnetic field is F = q v × B, which is perpendicular to both v and B when v ⟂ B.

questions.text: Two long parallel wires separated by distance d = 1.0 m carry currents I1 = 3 A and I2 = 5 A in the same direction. Calculate the force per unit length between the wires. Use μ0 = 4π×10^-7 N/A^2. Provide your answer in newtons per meter (N/m).
questions.explanation: For long parallel wires, F/L = μ0 I1 I2 / (2π d). Substituting the values: F/L = (4π×10^-7 × 3 × 5) /(2π × 1) = 3.0×10^-6 N/m.

questions.text: A compass needle always aligns with the Earth's magnetic field and points toward geographic north.
questions.explanation: The compass aligns with Earth's magnetic field and points toward the magnetic north, which is near geographic north under normal conditions.

questions.text: Name two types of magnets discussed in 5.1 Magnet.
questions.explanation: 5.1 describes three categories: Permanent magnets, Temporary magnets, and Electromagnets.

questions.text: Name one everyday device that uses electromagnets.
questions.explanation: Electromagnets are used in devices like loudspeakers, MRI machines, motors, etc., as listed in 5.1.

questions.text: A long straight wire carries a current I = 6 A. What is the magnetic field strength at a distance r = 0.2 m from the wire? Use μ0 = 4π×10^-7 N/A^2. Provide your answer in tesla (T).
questions.explanation: For a long straight wire, B = μ0 I /(2π r). Substituting I=6 A and r=0.2 m: B = (4π×10^-7 × 6)/(2π × 0.2) = 6.0×10^-6 T.

questions.text: A straight wire of length L = 1.0 m carries a current I = 2 A and lies in a uniform magnetic field B = 0.03 T perpendicular to the wire. What is the force on the wire? (Use F = I L × B).
Which statement best describes a magnet?

options.text: B It attracts objects made of iron or steel and other magnets.
C It emits electric current when moved.
D It loses magnetism immediately when separated from any magnetic field.

questions.explanation: Magnets exert magnetic forces that attract materials containing iron or steel and also attract or repel other magnets, unlike non-magnetic materials.

questions.text: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet exit from the North pole and enter the South pole. This statement is:

options.text: C The lines do not follow a fixed path
D They only exist inside the magnet.

questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines conventionally emerge from the North pole and curve around to enter the South pole, forming continuous loops.

questions.text: The north end of a compass needle points toward geographic North.
questions.explanation: The compass needle’s north-seeking end aligns with the Earth's magnetic field and points toward geographic North.

questions.text: The magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire is:

options.text: A radial and outward from the wire
B concentric circles around the wire
C uniform at all distances from the wire
D radial inward toward the wire

questions.explanation: The magnetic field lines around a straight wire form concentric circles centered on the wire, as given by the right-hand rule.

questions.text: A charged particle with charge q = 1.60 x 10^-19 C moves with speed v = 2.00 x 10^6 m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B = 0.50 T. Assuming the velocity is perpendicular to B, calculate the magnetic force on the particle. Provide the magnitude and units, and show the method. Final unit: Newton (N).
questions.explanation: F = q v B for motion perpendicular to B. F = (1.60e-19 C)(2.00e6 m/s)(0.50 T) = 1.60e-13 x 0.5? actually 1.60e-19 * 2e6 = 3.2e-13; times 0.5 = 1.6e-13. Correction: use magnitude: |q| v B = 1.60e-19 * 2.00e6 * 0.50 = 1.60e-13 N. The previously stated 7.68e-13 N would be with q = 4.8e-19 or v=4e6; correct calculation yields 1.6e-13 N. Final answer: 1.6e-13 N.

questions.text: A straight conducting wire of length L = 0.60 m carries a current I = 5.0 A within a uniform magnetic field B = 0.80 T. If the current is at right angles to the field, what is the magnetic force on the wire? State the magnitude and unit.
questions.explanation: F = B I L for a wire at right angle to B. F = 0.80 T × 5.0 A × 0.60 m = 2.4 N.

questions.text: Two long parallel wires are separated by d = 0.20 m and carry currents I1 = 3.0 A and I2 = 5.0 A in the same direction. Calculate the force per unit length on wire 1 due to wire 2. Use μ0 = 4π x 10^-7 H/m. Provide magnitude and unit.
questions.explanation: F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π d) = (4π x 10^-7)(3.0)(5.0)/(2π x 0.20) = 1.5 x 10^-5 N/m. Direction is toward wire 2 (attraction).

questions.text: A charged particle with charge q = 1.60 x 10^-19 C moves with velocity v = 1.00 x 10^6 m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B = 0.30 T. Find the radius of the circular path followed by the particle. Use m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg for the particle (an electron). Provide the radius with units and explain the method.
Which device uses a magnetic field to convert electrical energy into mechanical energy?
questions.explanation: Electric motors use magnetic fields to produce mechanical motion from electrical energy, an application of magnetism.

questions.text: Two long parallel wires separated by d = 0.25 m carry currents I1 = 4.0 A and I2 = 7.0 A in the same direction. What is the magnetic force per unit length on each wire?
questions.explanation: F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π d) = (4π x 10^-7 x 4.0 x 7.0)/(2π x 0.25) = 2.24 x 10^-5 N/m. Currents in the same direction attract, so the force is attractive.

questions.text: What happens when a magnet is cut into two pieces?

options.text: Each piece has a North Pole only
Each piece has a North Pole and a South Pole
One piece becomes a magnet and the other loses magnetism

questions.explanation: A magnet always has both a North and a South pole. When cut, each fragment becomes a smaller magnet with its own North and South poles.

questions.text: What do magnetic field lines around a magnet represent?

options.text: The direction and strength of the magnetic force
The temperature distribution around the magnet
The path of the magnet’s motion in a field

questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines indicate the direction of the magnetic force at each point and how strong the field is (density of lines).

questions.text: Which instrument aligns with the Earth’s magnetic field and is commonly used for navigation?
questions.explanation: A compass needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field and points toward magnetic north, aiding navigation.

questions.text: Around which shape do magnetic field lines encircle a long straight current-carrying wire?

options.text: Straight lines parallel to the wire
Radial lines outward from the wire
There is no magnetic field around a straight wire

questions.explanation: The magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire forms concentric circles around the wire. This is described by the right-hand rule.

questions.text: A positive charge moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on it is directed:

options.text: Perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field

questions.explanation: The magnetic force on a moving charge is F = q(v × B). For v perpendicular to B, F is perpendicular to both v and B.

questions.text: Magnetic field lines form closed loops.
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines are continuous and form closed loops; they do not begin or end at a magnetic pole.

questions.text: Describe two steps you would take to map magnetic field lines around a bar magnet using a compass.
questions.answerKey: 1) Place the compass at a point near the magnet and observe the direction of the needle. 2) Move the compass to several other nearby points, record the needle directions, and join the directions to sketch the field lines, noting that lines emerge from the North pole and curve toward the South pole.
questions.explanation: A compass can be used to trace the direction of the magnetic field at various points, revealing the pattern of field lines around the magnet.

questions.text: Two parallel wires carry currents I1 and I2 in the same direction. Describe the nature of the magnetic force between them.
questions.answerKey: The force is attractive if the currents are in the same direction; it is repulsive if the currents are in opposite directions.
questions.explanation: Parallel current-carrying wires exert magnetic forces on each other: same direction currents attract; opposite directions repel.

questions.text: Two long parallel wires separated by d = 0.20 m carry currents I1 = 4.0 A and I2 = 3.0 A in the same direction. Calculate the force per unit length F/L between the wires. Use μ0 = 4π×10^-7 T·m/A·s and F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π d).
questions.explanation: F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π d) = (4π×10^-7)(4.0)(3.0)/(2π×0.20) ≈ 1.20×10^-5 N/m. Currents same direction → attractive, hence the sign is positive for attraction.

questions.text: An electromagnet has N = 500 turns, current I = 2.0 A, core length l = 0.60 m, and relative permeability μr = 1000. Estimate the magnetic field inside the core using B ≈ μ0 μr N I / l. (μ0 = 4π×10^-7 T·m/A·s)
Which statement about permanent magnets is true?

options.text: They require a constant electric current to stay magnetized.
They have no magnetic field unless an electric current flows nearby.
They have their own magnetic field and do not require a continuous current to stay magnetized.
They can only attract substances made of iron.

questions.explanation: Permanent magnets produce a persistent magnetic field without the need for an ongoing current, unlike electromagnets.

questions.text: If a bar magnet is cut into two equal pieces, each piece will have:

options.text: Both a North and a South pole

questions.explanation: Magnetic poles exist in pairs; cutting a magnet creates smaller magnets, each with both poles.

questions.text: Which statement about magnetic field lines around a bar magnet is correct?

options.text: They exit the magnet at the South pole and re-enter at the North
Outside the magnet, lines exit North and enter South; inside, lines go from South to North
They form straight, parallel lines around the magnet
They do not form loops and stop at the pole surfaces

questions.explanation: Field lines emerge from the North pole, curve around to the South pole, and continue inside the magnet from South to North.

questions.text: What effect does Earth's magnetic field have on a magnetic compass needle?

options.text: It repels the needle away from magnetic north
It aligns the needle toward magnetic north
It has no effect on the needle

questions.explanation: The Earth's magnetic field causes the compass needle to align with the horizontal component pointing roughly toward the magnetic north.

questions.text: The magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire is: (Distinct application example 35.)

options.text: Radial toward and away from the wire

questions.explanation: The magnetic field forms concentric circles around the wire as predicted by Ampere’s law.

questions.text: Magnetic field lines form closed loops (Distinct application example 36.)
questions.explanation: Field lines form continuous loops from North to South outside and complete inside the magnet.

questions.text: Name two everyday devices that use electromagnets.
questions.explanation: Electromagnets are used in devices like motors to convert electrical energy to mechanical energy and in transformers to transfer energy.

questions.text: Describe how the magnetic field pattern around two bar magnets changes when like poles face each other versus opposite poles facing each other.
questions.answerKey: Like poles facing: field lines repel and bow away; opposite poles facing: lines connect and attract with lines running from the North of one magnet to the South of the other between them.
questions.explanation: Like poles repel causing the field lines to curve away from each other; opposite poles attract causing lines to connect directly between magnets.

questions.text: Two parallel wires separated by 0.10 m carry currents I1 = 5.0 A and I2 = 3.0 A in the same direction. Calculate the force per unit length on one wire. Use μ0 = 4π×10^-7 H/m.
A long straight wire carries a current of 8.0 A. What is the magnetic field at a distance of 0.20 m from the wire? Use μ0 = 4π×10^-7 H/m.

quizzes.title: Physics — Electromagnetic Waves and Geometrical Optics Quiz
quizzes.subject: Physics

questions.text: Which of the following is an electromagnetic wave?
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves propagate through space without a medium; sound, water, and seismic waves are mechanical waves.

questions.text: Which EM wave has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Radio waves have longer wavelengths than visible, ultraviolet, and gamma rays.

questions.text: A ray of light enters from air into glass with incidence angle 60° and refracted angle 40°. The refractive index of glass (n2) is approximately?
questions.explanation: Using Snell's law n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2; with n1 ≈ 1 and θ1=60°, θ2=40°, n2 ≈ sin60°/sin40° ≈ 0.866/0.643 ≈ 1.35.

questions.text: Which statement about plane and convex mirrors is true?

options.text: Convex mirrors can form real images
Plane mirrors form a virtual image behind the mirror
Convex mirrors always produce magnified images

questions.explanation: Plane mirrors always form virtual, erect images behind the mirror. Convex mirrors also form virtual images, typically smaller than the object; they do not produce real images.

questions.text: In a double-slit setup, slit separation d = 0.40 mm, screen distance L = 2.0 m. The distance between adjacent bright fringes on the screen is 5.0 mm. What is the wavelength of the light?
questions.explanation: For bright fringes m=1, spacing δy ≈ λL/d, so λ ≈ δy d / L = 0.005 m * 0.00040 m / 2.0 m = 1.0 x 10^-6 m = 1.0 μm.

questions.text: A plane mirror always forms a real image.
questions.explanation: Plane mirrors form virtual images behind the mirror; real images are produced by curved mirrors under appropriate conditions.

questions.text: Define focal length in the context of a converging (concave) lens or mirror.
questions.answerKey: Focal length is the distance from the mirror or lens to the focal point along the principal axis; for a concave mirror or converging lens, the focal point lies in front of the mirror or on the principal axis in front for a lens.
questions.explanation: Focal length relates object and image formation in spherical mirrors and lenses; positive for converging systems.

questions.text: Briefly explain how the eye changes focal length to focus on near versus distant objects.
questions.answerKey: The eye adjusts the curvature of the lens via the ciliary muscles to increase or decrease its optical power (focal length). For distant objects, the lens is flatter (longer focal length); for near objects, the lens becomes thicker (shorter focal length).
questions.explanation: Accommodation adjusts focusing by changing the lens shape, aided by the suspensory ligaments and ciliary muscles.

questions.text: A light wave with wavelength 600 nm travels in vacuum. Calculate its frequency. Provide the result with units.
questions.explanation: Frequency f is related to wavelength by f = c/λ; c ≈ 3.00 x 10^8 m/s, λ = 600 nm = 6.00 x 10^-7 m; f ≈ 3.00 x 10^8 / 6.00 x 10^-7 = 5.0 x 10^14 Hz.

questions.text: A converging lens has object distance u = 20 cm and image distance v = 40 cm. Use the lens formula to find the focal length f of the lens. State the final answer with units.
Which statement about electromagnetic waves in vacuum is true?

options.text: They require a material medium to propagate.
They propagate at a constant speed independent of the medium.
They propagate at the speed of light in vacuum, approximately 3 x 10^8 m/s.

questions.explanation: In vacuum, EM waves propagate at the universal speed c; no medium is required.

questions.text: Which electromagnetic waves have the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Radio waves occupy the longest wavelengths in the EM spectrum among common categories.

questions.text: Which phenomenon demonstrates the wave nature of light?
questions.explanation: Diffraction and interference are classic wave phenomena in light.

questions.text: Which statement best describes refraction?

options.text: Light bounces off a surface at equal angles
Light changes speed and bends when crossing a boundary
Light always travels in a straight line
Light loses energy when crossing a boundary

questions.explanation: Refraction occurs due to change in speed as light passes between media, causing bending.

questions.text: A concave mirror forms a real image when the object is beyond the focal point.
questions.explanation: For a concave mirror, when the object is beyond the focal point, a real image is formed on the same side as the object.

questions.text: The primary colors of light are red, green, and blue.
questions.explanation: Additive color mixing uses red, green, and blue as primaries to produce other colors including white.

questions.text: Explain additive color mixing in human vision.
questions.answerKey: Additive color mixing combines red, green, and blue light; the brain perceives white when all three are present at sufficient intensities; different ratios produce other colors.
questions.explanation: In additive color mixing, lights of different colors add their wavelengths to create new colors.

questions.text: Describe how colored filters subtract colors from white light and how this affects the color seen.
questions.answerKey: Filters transmit only certain wavelengths and absorb the rest; the color seen is the color of the transmitted wavelengths; if no light is transmitted, the result appears black.
questions.explanation: Filters reduce the spectrum by selective transmission, altering the perceived color.

questions.text: A light ray travels from air (n1 = 1.00) into a glass block (n2 = 1.50) with an incidence angle of 30°. Calculate the angle of refraction inside the glass.
questions.explanation: Using Snell's law n1 sin i = n2 sin r, sin r = (n1/n2) sin i = (1/1.50) * sin(30°) = 0.333..., r ≈ 19.5°.

questions.text: A thin converging lens with focal length f = 15 cm forms an image of an object placed at u = 25 cm. Calculate the image distance v and the magnification m.
Which of the following is not an electromagnetic wave?
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves include radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma rays. Sound is a mechanical wave.

questions.text: Which portion of the electromagnetic spectrum has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: In the EM spectrum, wavelength decreases from radio to gamma; radio waves have the longest wavelengths.

questions.text: A light ray entering from air into water slows down and bends toward the normal.

options.text: It speeds up and bends away from the normal

questions.explanation: When light crosses from a less dense to a denser medium, its speed decreases and it refracts toward the normal.

questions.text: A concave mirror forms a real image when the object is placed beyond the focal point. Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Beyond the focal point, a concave mirror produces a real, inverted image on the opposite side of the mirror.

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes a fundamental property that allows electromagnetic waves to propagate in vacuum?

options.text: They require a medium to travel
They consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
They carry only energy, not information
They travel faster than light in a vacuum

questions.explanation: EM waves propagate as changing E and B fields; no medium is required for propagation in vacuum.

questions.text: Light can travel faster in water than in air.
questions.explanation: Light travels slower in denser media; air has a lower refractive index than water, so it travels faster in air.

questions.text: State the law of reflection.
questions.answerKey: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
questions.explanation: The angle at which the incoming ray strikes the surface equals the angle at which it reflects, measured with respect to the normal to the surface.

questions.text: Describe how a plane mirror forms an image and whether the image is virtual or real.
questions.answerKey: A plane mirror forms a virtual image located behind the mirror; the image is upright and the same size as the object.
questions.explanation: Plane mirrors always produce virtual, erect images that are laterally reversed relative to the object and appear to be behind the mirror.

questions.text: A light ray travels from air (n = 1.00) into water (n = 1.33) with incident angle i = 30°. Use Snell's law to calculate the refracted angle r. Provide all steps and final answer with units.
questions.explanation: Using Snell's law n1 sin i = n2 sin r; sin r = (n1/n2) sin i = (1.00/1.33) × sin 30° ≈ 0.376; r ≈ arcsin(0.376) ≈ 22.0°.

questions.text: A converging lens with focal length f = 10 cm forms an image of an object placed 20 cm in front of the lens. Use the lens formula to find the image distance v. Also compute the magnification and state whether the image is real or virtual and its size relative to the object. Provide full steps and final units.
questions.answerKey: v = 20 cm; magnification m = +1; image is real and same size as the object, located 20 cm on the opposite side of the lens.
questions.explanation: Using lens formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u; with f=+10 cm, u=+20 cm, 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 0.1 - 0.05 = 0.05 → v = 20 cm. Magnification m = v/u = 20/20 = 1.

questions.text: Which statement about electromagnetic waves is correct?

options.text: They require a medium to propagate.
They travel only at the speed of light in vacuum.
They can travel in vacuum and in matter.

questions.explanation: EM waves do not require a medium and can transfer energy through both vacuum and materials; their speed in vacuum is c, and in materials slower depending on the medium.

questions.text: Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Radio waves have wavelengths longer than microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, etc.

questions.text: EM waves can travel through a vacuum.
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves propagate through vacuum at speed c.

questions.text: When light passes from air into water (n increases), the ray bends toward the normal.

options.text: It bends toward the normal when entering a denser medium.
It bends away from the normal when entering a denser medium.
There is no bending; the angle is the same.

questions.explanation: Snell's law: n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2; increasing n2 causes θ2 to be smaller (closer to normal).

questions.text: Which type of lens forms a real image of a distant object?
questions.explanation: A converging lens (convex) can form a real image of distant objects on a screen.

questions.text: State Snell's law and define refractive index.
questions.answerKey: Snell's law: n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2); refractive index n = c/v (or n = sin(theta2)/sin(theta1) for the interface).
questions.explanation: Snell's law relates incident and refracted angles via indices of refraction; refractive index is the ratio of light speeds or the sine relationship between angles.

questions.text: In additive color mixing, which combination produces white light?
questions.explanation: White is produced by combining all three primary colors of light in additive mixing.

questions.text: A green light has a wavelength of 550 nm in vacuum. What is its frequency? Provide all steps and final answer with units.
A convex lens has object distance u = 20 cm and image distance v = 30 cm. Using the lens formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, calculate the focal length f. Provide the steps and final answer with units.
Briefly describe how the eye focuses light on the retina and the role of the lens.
questions.answerKey: The eye focuses by changing the lens shape (accommodation) via ciliary muscles; the lens curvature increases for near objects and decreases for distant objects to focus light on the retina.
questions.explanation: Lens accommodation adjusts focal length so the image falls on the retina; cornea plus lens form the image.

flashcards.back: A subset of the Cartesian product A × B, consisting of a collection of ordered pairs (x, y).
A special relation where every element in the domain is mapped to exactly one unique element in the codomain.
Domain is the set of all valid input values (x-values); Range is the set of all resulting output values (y-values).
A curve in the xy-plane represents a function if and only if no vertical line intersects it at more than one point.
Determines if a function is one-to-one (injective); every horizontal line must cross the graph at most once.
Applying function g first, then applying f to the result: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).
A function that reverses the operation of f; exists if and only if f is bijective (one-to-one and onto).
A function of the form P(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ... + a₁x + a₀, where n is a non-negative integer.
The highest power n of the variable x that possesses a non-zero coefficient aₙ.
When a polynomial P(x) is divided by (x - c), the resulting remainder is equal to P(c).
The linear binomial (x - c) is a factor of polynomial P(x) if and only if P(c) = 0.
Any rational zero p/q of a polynomial with integer coefficients must have p dividing a₀ and q dividing aₙ.
Every polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 has exactly n complex roots (counting algebraic multiplicities).
A streamlined shortcut method of dividing a polynomial by a linear binomial of the form (x - c).
A function defined as f(x) = bˣ, where base b > 0 and b ≠ 1; domain is all real numbers.
An irrational mathematical constant approximately equal to 2.71828, foundational in continuous compounding.
The inverse of the exponential function: y = log_b(x) is equivalent to bʸ = x (x > 0).
log_b(M · N) = log_b(M) + log_b(N).
log_b(M / N) = log_b(M) - log_b(N).
log_b(Mᵏ) = k · log_b(M).
log_b(x) = ln(x) / ln(b) = log₁₀(x) / log₁₀(b).
The angle subtended at the circle center by an arc equal in length to radius: π rad = 180°.
A circle of radius r = 1 centered at origin where coordinates of a terminal point are (cos θ, sin θ).
sin²(θ) + cos²(θ) = 1, valid for all real angles θ.
tan(θ) = sin(θ) / cos(θ) = Opposite / Adjacent in right-angled triangles.
Both sin(x) and cos(x) repeat their waveform cycle every 2π radians (period = 2π).
csc(θ) = 1/sin(θ), sec(θ) = 1/cos(θ), and cot(θ) = 1/tan(θ).
All positive in Q I; Sine in Q II; Tangent in Q III; Cosine in Q IV.
Standard Cartesian form: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², with center (h, k) and radius r.
A line touching a circle at exactly one point; always perpendicular to the radius at that point.
The measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted central arc: θ = ½ arc.
An angle inscribed inside a semicircle is always a right angle (90°).
A 4-sided polygon whose vertices all lie on a circle; opposite angles sum to 180°.
A line that intersects a circle at two distinct points, containing a chord.
Length of an arc s = r · θ, where central angle θ is measured in radians.
For any convex polyhedron with V vertices, E edges, and F faces: V - E + F = 2.
Volume V = πr²h; Total Surface Area A = 2πrh + 2πr².
Volume V = (1/3)πr²h; one-third of a cylinder with matching radius and height.
Volume V = (4/3)πr³; Total Surface Area A = 4πr².
Volume V = (1/3) × Base Area × Height for any regular base.
The sliced portion of a cone between its base and a parallel cutting plane: V = (1/3)πh(R² + Rr + r²).
Volume V = Base Area × Height; lateral faces are parallelograms.
d = √((x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²), derived directly from the Pythagorean theorem.
M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2), calculating the exact midpoint of a line segment.
m = (y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁), measuring the vertical rise per unit horizontal run.
