Decisive victory of Ethiopian patriotic forces under Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu over Italian invaders, preserving independence.
Disputed treaty between Menelik and Italy; deceptive Article XVII Italian text claimed an Italian protectorate, sparking war.
Founded Addis Ababa (1886), introduced modern schools, telecommunications, postal system, banks, and the Franco-Ethiopian railway.
Mussolini's unprovoked invasion using banned mustard poison gas, culminating in brief occupation of major urban centers (1936–1941).
Ethiopian patriotic resistance fighters who waged relentless rural guerrilla warfare against fascist occupation until liberation in 1941.
Triggered in June 1914 by the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary by Gavrilo Princip in Sarajevo.
Defensive combat along the Western Front where opposing armies occupied fortified trenches separated by barbed wire 'No Man's Land'.
Post-WWI peace treaty punishing Germany with war guilt clause 231, territory loss, disarming, and colossal financial reparations.
International diplomatic body formed in 1919 to maintain collective security; failed due to lack of military power and appeasement.
Authoritarian totalitarian movements under Benito Mussolini (Italy) and Adolf Hitler (Germany) combining militarism and extreme nationalism.
Began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany launched Blitzkrieg invasion of Poland, prompting Britain and France to declare war.
Emperor Haile Selassie's historic address at Geneva warning that international abandonment of Ethiopia would invite global catastrophe.
Decades-long geopolitical and ideological confrontation between the capitalist USA and communist USSR (1945–1991).
Established in San Francisco post-WWII with 51 charter member states (including sovereign Ethiopia) to safeguard global peace.
Forum formed in Belgrade in 1961 by developing states refusing military alignment with either superpower Cold War bloc.
32 independent African states established the Organization of African Unity in Addis Ababa to eradicate colonialism and unite Africa.
Rapid collapse of European empires following WWII as nationalist liberation movements achieved sovereign independence across continents.
US financial aid initiative providing over $12 billion to rebuild war-shattered Western European industrial economies after 1947.
Opposing Cold War military defense alliances: North Atlantic Treaty Organization (1949) vs the Soviet Warsaw Pact (1955).
Emperor Haile Selassie returned to Addis Ababa on May 5, 1941, restoring imperial administration with initial British military assistance.
University students mobilized in the 1960s challenging imperial autocracy and feudal tenancy under the slogan 'Land to the Tiller!'.
Mass protests, urban strikes, and military mutinies culminated in the Derg deposing Emperor Haile Selassie on September 12, 1974.
The Derg nationalized all rural land without compensation, abolishing feudal landlordism and redistributing plots to peasant associations.
Brutal state-sponsored violent campaign waged by the Derg regime (1976–1978) against urban political opposition groups like the EPRP.
Invasion of eastern Ethiopia by Siad Barre's Somali army, repelled by Ethiopian armed forces with Soviet and Cuban military logistics.
After protracted civil war, insurgent coalition forces of the EPRDF captured Addis Ababa, ending Colonel Mengistu Hailemariam's regime.
Historic milestone when seventeen African nations achieved formal political independence from British, French, and Belgian colonial rule.
Institutionalized racist system of white minority supremacy and racial segregation dismantled through ANC resistance and global boycotts.
Anti-apartheid revolutionary imprisoned for 27 years who was elected South Africa's first democratic multi-racial President in 1994.
Philosophical movement fostering continental solidarity led by visionary figures like Kwame Nkrumah, Julius Nyerere, and Jomo Kenyatta.
The OAU transformed into the African Union in Durban, South Africa, prioritizing economic integration, peace operations, and good governance.
The African Union's 50-year strategic framework for inclusive sustainable development, continental integration, and economic renaissance.
Coups d'état, external debt burdens, border disputes, and structural adjustment programs navigated by newly sovereign states.
Ratified in December 1994, established a federal democratic republic recognizing the unconditional self-determination of Ethiopian nationalities.
Following a UN-supervised referendum in April 1993, Eritrea formally declared sovereign independence from Ethiopia.
Devastating border conflict centered on Badme, culminating in the Algiers Peace Agreement signed in December 2000.
Massive expansion of national highways, hydroelectric dams, rural electrification, and higher education universities across all regions.
Leadership transition bringing release of political prisoners, peace rapprochement with Eritrea, and economic liberalization measures.
Administrative organization of Ethiopia into regional states based on settlement patterns, language, and consent of peoples.
Establishment of national commissions to foster inclusive political consensus and sustainable peaceful coexistence across communities.
Enormous monolithic granite stelae carved and erected in Aksum during the 3rd–4th centuries CE marking underground royal tombs.
Eleven UNESCO World Heritage monolithic churches chiseled out of solid volcanic rock in the 12th–13th century under King Lalibela.
Indigenous socio-political generation-class system of the Oromo people inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
Fortified imperial compound in Gondar built by Emperor Fasilides and successors in the 17th century combining European, Arab, and Axumite styles.
Historic walled Islamic center with 82 mosques and 102 shrines, recognized by UNESCO as the fourth holiest city of Islam.
Archaeological site in central Ethiopia containing 36 carved anthropomorphic stone megaliths dating back to the 12th–14th century.
Centuries-old botanical pharmacopeia utilized by indigenous healers to treat human and livestock ailments using indigenous herbs.
Sport fosters social integration, community solidarity, interpersonal communication, civic discipline, and stress reduction.
Won the 1960 Rome Olympic marathon running barefoot, becoming the first black African to win an Olympic gold medal.
Cultural heritage games such as Genna (traditional field hockey), Gugs (horseback spear tournament), and Qille.
Promoting equal athletic opportunities, facilities, and leadership roles for girls and women, eradicating cultural barriers.
Utilizing athletic tournaments to bring divided communities together, fostering mutual empathy and peaceful coexistence.
Sports industry generates employment for coaches, athletes, equipment manufacturers, and promotes national tourism.
Adapted physical education and Paralympic sports ensuring athletic access and dignity for individuals of all abilities.
The capacity of the heart and lungs to deliver oxygen-rich blood to working muscles during sustained physical exertion.
Strength is the maximal force a muscle can generate in a single effort; endurance is the ability to sustain repeated contractions.
The anatomical range of motion available at a joint or group of joints without experiencing pain or tissue injury.
Framework for exercise prescription: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), and Type (exercise mode).
Optimal aerobic exercise intensity zone, generally between 60% and 85% of estimated maximum heart rate (220 - age).
The relative proportion of fat mass to lean tissue (muscle, bone, water) in the human body, assessed via BMI or skinfolds.
Warm-up prepares muscles and elevates heart rate to prevent injury; cool-down restores resting circulatory homeostasis.
Short-distance maximum velocity races (100m, 200m, 400m) run in assigned lanes utilizing starting blocks.
Middle distance (800m, 1,500m) and long distance (5,000m, 10,000m, Marathon), where Ethiopia holds legendary world dominance.
Passing the baton between teammates inside the designated 20m takeover box using blind/non-visual exchanges in 4×100m.
Horizontal jumps (Long Jump and Triple Jump) and vertical jumps (High Jump using Fosbury Flop, and Pole Vault).
Shot Put (glide or rotational technique), Discus Throw, Javelin Throw, and Hammer Throw from circular circles or runways.
Sprint hurdles (110m hurdles for men, 100m for women, and 400m hurdles) demanding sprint speed and rhythmic obstacle clearance.
Oxidative phosphorylation utilizing glycogen and fats to produce cellular ATP during sustained endurance races.
Played on a rectangular pitch (100–110m length) by two competing teams of 11 players each, including one designated goalkeeper.
A player is offside if closer to opponent's goal line than both ball and second-last opponent when ball is played to them.
Direct free kick can score a goal immediately without another touch; indirect free kick must touch another player first.
Awarded when a defending player commits a direct free kick offense inside their own penalty area; taken from 11 meters.
Push pass (inside of foot for short accuracy), instep driven pass (long balls), and lofted chip passes.
Using various foot surfaces to maneuver past defenders while maintaining close peripheral ball control and vision.
Enforces the 17 Laws of the Game, issues cautionary yellow or red cards, and maintains control of player safety.
18m × 9m court divided by a center net (height: 2.43m for men, 2.24m for women) with an attack line 3 meters from net.
Teams are allowed up to 3 consecutive ball touches before sending over the net, typically: Pass/Bump → Set → Spike.
Players rotate clockwise through positions 1 through 6 each time their team wins back the right to serve (side-out).
Joining hands and extending forearms to create a flat rebound platform for controlling incoming serves and hard spikes.
Using soft finger pads above the forehead to deliver a high, accurate ball for an attacking teammate to spike.
Defensive back-row specialist wearing a contrasting jersey who cannot serve, block, or attack above net height.
A point is scored on every single rally regardless of which team served; sets are won at 25 points (win by 2).
Played by two teams of 5 court players aiming to score by shooting the ball through a hoop elevated 3.05 meters (10 feet).
Field goals inside arc = 2 points; shots behind perimeter arc = 3 points; uncontested foul free throws = 1 point each.
Taking more than two steps without dribbling the ball, resulting in immediate turnover of possession.
Dribbling with both hands at once, or restarting a dribble after coming to a complete stop.
FIBA rule requiring the offensive team to attempt a field goal hitting the rim within 24 seconds of possessing the ball.
Zone defense assigns players to guard specific floor areas; man-to-man assigns each defender to guard a specific opponent.
Illegal physical contact (holding, pushing, charging); a player with 5 fouls (FIBA) is disqualified from the game.
40m × 20m court contested by 7 active players per team (6 outfield players plus 1 goalkeeper) with 3m × 2m goals.
Players may hold the ball for a maximum of 3 seconds and take up to 3 steps before passing, bouncing, or shooting.
Only the goalkeeper is permitted inside the 6m D-zone; outfield attackers can jump and shoot before landing inside.
Taking off from one foot outside the 6-meter line, releasing the ball at peak jump height before contacting the floor.
Penalty for serious fouls or unsportsmanlike conduct; the penalized team must play with one fewer player for 2 minutes.
Referees raise a hand to warn against delaying an attack without attempting to score; ball must be shot within limited passes.
Awarded when a clear scoring chance is illegally destroyed by a defender anywhere on the court.
To preserve personal safety, cultivate situational awareness, avoid dangerous situations, and de-escalate confrontations.
Playing within established rules, honoring match officials, treating competitors with dignity, and valuing integrity above victory.
Strict prohibition of performance-enhancing drugs (anabolic steroids, EPO) to safeguard athlete health and equal competition.
Immediate acute sprain/strain first aid: Rest, Ice (15-20 min), Compression bandage, Elevation above heart level.
Gracious conduct in winning and losing, acknowledging great play by opponents, and fostering positive camaraderie.
Using calm, confident body language, neutral voice tone, and active listening to defuse verbal conflicts before physical violence.
Recognizing traumatic brain injury signs (dizziness, nausea, photophobia, confusion); immediate removal from play is mandatory.

flashcards.front: What is an isthmus, and what famous example connects North America to South America?
flashcards.back: An isthmus is a narrow strip of land with water on both sides connecting two larger pieces of land. A well-known example is the Isthmus of Panama.
flashcards.explanation: An isthmus connects two landmasses with water on two sides, whereas a peninsula is bordered by water on three sides.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of the World’s Major Landforms
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is the highest landform on Earth, what is its elevation, and where is it located?
flashcards.back: Mt. Everest; it stands at 8,849 meters above sea level in the Himalaya Mountain range between Nepal and Tibet.
flashcards.explanation: It was formed by continental collision between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of the World’s Major Landforms
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How many recognized sovereign states are located on the African continent?
flashcards.back: Africa is home to 54 recognized sovereign states.
flashcards.explanation: Africa is the second-largest continent in both areal size and total population after Asia.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Location and Related Features of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What are the four major landform regions of Africa listed in Table 1.1 of the textbook?
flashcards.back: 1. African Alpine System; 2. African Massif; 3. East African Highlands and Rift System; 4. Southern Africa Platform.
flashcards.explanation: These four major regions contain all eight physical sub-regions of Africa.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Landforms of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What does the Arabic word “Sahel” mean, and what type of geographical zone does it describe?
flashcards.back: “Sahel” means “shore”. It describes a 5,000 km semiarid transitional savanna/grassland belt along the southern edge of the Sahara Desert.
flashcards.explanation: The Sahel stretches west-to-east from Mauritania and Senegal all the way to Somalia.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Landforms of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Why are soils in the African tropical rainforest generally acidic and nutrient poor?
flashcards.back: High year-round rainfall causes extreme chemical weathering and leaching, washing essential nutrients out of the soil despite rapid organic decomposition.
flashcards.explanation: Frequent heavy rain leaches topsoil nutrients away even though organic matter breaks down rapidly.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Landforms of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is a graben, and how is it formed within a rift valley?
flashcards.back: A graben is an elongated block of the Earth's crust lying between two faults that is displaced downward relative to surrounding blocks.
flashcards.explanation: It is formed by normal faulting as tension pulls the Earth's crust in opposite directions.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Landforms of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Which ocean current contributed to the formation of the Namib Desert along the west coast of Namibia?
flashcards.back: The cold Benguela Ocean Current.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook attributes the Namib’s formation partly to the nearby cold Benguela Current.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Landforms of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What empirical data did Wladimir Köppen use to establish his world climate classification scheme?
flashcards.back: Mean monthly and annual values of temperature and precipitation, believing that natural vegetation best expresses overall climate.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook associates Groups A, C, D, and E with temperature, Group B with precipitation, and Highland group H with altitude.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of World Climatic Regions and Types
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What are the four major global climate zones and their latitudinal boundaries?
flashcards.back: Tropical Zone (0°–23.5°); Subtropics Zone (23.5°–40°); Temperate Zone (40°–60°); Cold Zone (60°–90°).
flashcards.explanation: The textbook divides the zones by latitude and relates their conditions to incoming solar radiation and angle of incidence.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of World Climatic Regions and Types
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What are the main temperature and precipitation characteristics of the Equatorial Climate Region in Africa?
flashcards.back: High average temperatures (~26°C) year-round, low diurnal temperature range (~3°C), heavy cloud cover, high humidity, and heavy convectional rainfall.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook names March and September as the hottest months, when the Sun is overhead at the Equator; it does not call them peak-rainfall months.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Climate Types and Zones of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is the Harmattan, and what atmospheric conditions does it bring to West Africa?
flashcards.back: A warm, dry northeasterly or easterly wind blowing out of the southern Sahara during the low-sun (winter) season, often carrying sand and dust.
flashcards.explanation: The cited passage describes the Harmattan as warm and dry, not cool, and notes its dust and sand during the low-sun season.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Climate Types and Zones of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How does the seasonal movement of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) affect rainfall in Africa?
flashcards.back: The ITCZ moves north to ~13°N in June (northern summer) and south along West Africa to Madagascar in December (northern winter), drawing rain-bearing wind convergence along its path.
flashcards.explanation: Migration of the ITCZ closely controls the seasonal distribution of rainfall and symmetrical climate zones across Africa.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Climate Types and Zones of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is the Environmental Lapse Rate stated in the textbook, and how does altitude affect temperatures?
flashcards.back: Air temperature decreases with altitude at an average rate of 6.4°C per 1,000 meters.
flashcards.explanation: This lapse rate explains why elevated plateaus like the Ethiopian Highlands are cool and high peaks like Mt. Kilimanjaro have permanent snow cover.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Climate Types and Zones of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How does persistent climate change directly impact surface and river water supplies in Africa?
flashcards.back: It leads to shrinkage in surface-water supplies and reduces the quantity and regularity of streams and river flows.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook links stream levels, river flow, and underground water to climate types and water availability; it says persistent climate change may shrink surface-water supply and reduce stream and river quantity and regularity.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Benefits of Climate for Life of People of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What key factors drive Africa's high vulnerability to climate change according to the textbook?
flashcards.back: Weak adaptive capacity, high dependence on ecosystem goods for livelihoods, and less-developed agricultural production systems.
flashcards.explanation: The cited section lists these factors and links climate change to risks for agricultural production, food security, water resources, and ecosystem services.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Climate Change and its Challenges to Africa’s Development Vision
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is “sustainable use” of natural resources as defined in the textbook?
flashcards.back: Using resources in a way and at a rate that avoids long-term environmental degradation, preserving their potential to meet the needs of both present and future generations.
flashcards.explanation: Sustainable resource management balances current human utilization with long-term ecological preservation.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of Major Natural Resources of the World
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What percentage of total global water is freshwater, and where is the vast majority of it stored?
flashcards.back: Freshwater makes up only 2.5% of all Earth water; 68.7% of that freshwater is locked in glaciers and permanent snow, and 30.1% is stored as groundwater.
flashcards.explanation: Table 3.1 lists freshwater in lakes at 0.26% and in rivers at 0.006% of the freshwater total.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of Major Natural Resources of the World
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is the technical difference between a drainage basin and a watershed?
flashcards.back: A drainage basin is an area where surface water from rain converges to a single point at lower elevation; a watershed is a divide separating one drainage area from another.
flashcards.explanation: The basin is the catchment area itself; the watershed is the boundary line separating basins.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Drainage and Water Resources in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What distinguishes the Chad Basin from all other major river basins in Africa?
flashcards.back: The Chad Basin is the largest inland drainage area in Africa; its main water body is shallow Lake Chad, whose size varies seasonally.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook places Lake Chad in the semiarid Sahel and attributes high seasonal evaporation to the region’s high temperatures.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Drainage and Water Resources in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What are Leptosols, what proportion of African soils do they represent, and where do they typically form?
flashcards.back: Leptosols are shallow soils over hard rock or gravelly material comprising 17% of African soils; they occur mainly in desert and mountainous areas where physical rock disintegration prevails.
flashcards.explanation: Freeze/thaw and heating/cooling temperature cycles drive Leptosol formation on exposed rock.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Main Types of Soils and Mineral Resources in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Which two countries does the textbook say produce more than half the world’s cobalt?
flashcards.back: The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia.
flashcards.explanation: The text says the D.R. Congo and Zambia together produce more than half of world cobalt. Table 3.2 ranks the D.R. Congo first in 2019 cobalt mine production; 51.43% is in the table’s world-reserves column, not a production-share column.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Main Types of Soils and Mineral Resources in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What four primary environmental and biological factors dictate the spatial distribution of vegetation in Africa?
flashcards.back: Climate (temperature, precipitation, humidity, light, wind); landform (elevation, slope orientation, slope degree); soils (chemical composition and water capacity); and biotic factors (plant/animal interactions and competition).
flashcards.explanation: Vegetation distribution patterns closely mirror climate maps across the continent.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Vegetation and Wildlife of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is an endemic mammal, and what are four examples of endemic African mammals listed in the textbook?
flashcards.back: The textbook describes endemic African mammals as found nowhere else in the world; four listed examples are the Walia ibex, Nyala, giraffe, and hippopotamus.
flashcards.explanation: The cited passage says these mammals are endemic to Africa, meaning they are found nowhere else in the world.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Vegetation and Wildlife of Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: By mid-2020, what shares of the world population did Asia and Africa account for, and how large was Oceania’s population?
flashcards.back: Asia accounted for 59.4% and Africa for 17.5% of the world population. Oceania had about 43 million people (about 0.5% in Table 4.2).
flashcards.explanation: Asia was the most populous continent, Africa the second most populous, and Oceania the least populous in the cited mid-2020 comparison.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of World Population Growth and Size
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is the Demographic Balancing Equation, and what do its symbols mean?
flashcards.back: `Pₜ − P₀ = B − D + I − O`, or `Pₜ − P₀ = NI + NM`. `Pₜ` is population at the end of the period; `P₀` is population at the beginning; `B` = births; `D` = deaths; `I` = in-migration; `O` = out-migration; `NI = B − D` (natural increase); and `NM = I − O` (net migration).
flashcards.explanation: Population change is natural increase plus net migration; each component is defined on printed p. 95.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of World Population Growth and Size
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How does the textbook define Total Fertility Rate (TFR) and Crude Birth Rate (CBR), and what is the CBR formula?
flashcards.back: TFR is the average number of children a woman would give birth to during her lifetime if she experienced present-day age-specific fertility rates during childbearing years (15–49). `CBR = (total annual live births ÷ total mid-year population) × 1,000`.
flashcards.explanation: TFR is expressed as children per woman; CBR is annual live births per 1,000 of the mid-year population.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Africa’s Major Demographic Trends
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What are the textbook formulas for Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) and Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR)?
flashcards.back: `IMR = (annual infant deaths ÷ annual live births) × 1,000`. `MMR = (deaths due to maternal causes ÷ total annual live births) × 100,000`.
flashcards.explanation: IMR uses a base of 1,000 live births; MMR uses a base of 100,000 live births.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Africa’s Major Demographic Trends
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: According to Table 4.8, what were Africa’s 2020 young-, working-age-, and old-age population shares, and its listed age dependency ratio (ADR)?
flashcards.back: Young (ages 0–14): 41%; working age (15–64): 56%; old age (65+): 3%; ADR: 78.6 (the table column is labeled “Age Dependency Ratio (ADR) × 100”).
flashcards.explanation: The table lists the three age-group shares and an ADR of 78.6; it does not give an ADR calculation formula on this cited page.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Population Structure
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What three population-pyramid types does the textbook identify, and what are the key features of the expansive and stationary types?
flashcards.back: The textbook lists **Expansive**, **Constructive**, and **Stationary** pyramids. An expansive pyramid has a broad base, many children, rapid growth, and relatively few older people. A stationary pyramid has balanced fertility and mortality (`B = D`) and zero population growth.
flashcards.explanation: The cited page labels the second type **“Constructive Pyramid”**; the textbook describes stationary as balanced fertility and mortality.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Population Structure
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What was Africa’s average crude population density in mid-2019, and which countries does the textbook distinguish as most populous versus most densely populated?
flashcards.back: Africa’s average crude density was about 44 persons/km². Most populous: Nigeria, Ethiopia, Egypt, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the Republic of South Africa. Most densely populated: Mauritius, Rwanda, Burundi, Comoros, and Seychelles.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook cautions that a country can be populous without being densely populated; population size and density are different measures.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Distribution and Density of Africa’s Population
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Which country was least urbanized, which was near 90% urbanized, and how did the least- and most-urbanized regions compare?
flashcards.back: Burundi was least urbanized at 12%; Gabon was almost 90% urbanized. Eastern Africa was the least-urbanized region, while Southern Africa was the most urbanized; Table 4.10 gives 26% and 62%, respectively, in 2016.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook’s Table 4.10 contrasts Eastern Africa (26%) with Southern Africa (62%); the nearby text identifies Burundi (12%) and Gabon (almost 90%).
flashcards.sectionTitle: Urban and Rural Settlement Patterns in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What defines the Quaternary economic sector, and what types of activities does it include?
flashcards.back: The Quaternary sector is knowledge-based and focuses on generating and sharing information. Activities include information and communication technology (ICT), research and development, education, and financial planning.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook calls the Quaternary sector knowledge-based and lists those information-generating and information-sharing activities.
flashcards.unitTitle: Major Economic and Cultural Activities of Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of Employment Structure in the World
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How does the distribution of employment by sector differ between developed and developing countries?
flashcards.back: Developed countries have more people working in the tertiary (service) sector. Developing countries have more people working in the primary sector, particularly agriculture.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook says each sector’s share varies with level of development: developed countries have more tertiary-sector workers, while developing countries have more primary-sector workers, particularly in agriculture.
flashcards.unitTitle: Major Economic and Cultural Activities of Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of Employment Structure in the World
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What statistical contribution does agriculture make to employment, GDP, and exports in Africa?
flashcards.back: Agriculture employs about two-thirds of Africa’s working population, contributes on average 30–60% of GDP, and accounts for about 30% of each country’s export value.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook describes agriculture as Africa’s single most important economic activity and notes that most of it is rain-fed and vulnerable to climate variability.
flashcards.unitTitle: Major Economic and Cultural Activities of Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Economic Activities in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is “working poverty,” and what daily earnings threshold defines it in Africa?
flashcards.back: Working poverty refers to people who are employed but earn less than US$2 a day. The textbook says Africa has the world’s highest rate of working poverty.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook links working poverty to employed people remaining poor because of weak economic structures and low wages.
flashcards.unitTitle: Major Economic and Cultural Activities of Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Major Economic Activities in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How do voluntary and involuntary unemployment differ, and what is the formula for calculating the unemployment rate?
flashcards.back: Voluntary unemployment is joblessness by choice; involuntary unemployment is when a person is willing and able to work for a given wage but cannot find a job. Unemployment rate = (number of unemployed people ÷ total number of people in the workforce) × 100.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook distinguishes voluntary from involuntary unemployment and calculates the rate by dividing unemployed people by the total workforce, then multiplying by 100.
flashcards.unitTitle: Major Economic and Cultural Activities of Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Possible Solutions to the Problem of Unemployment
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How many flagship programs are established under Agenda 2063, and what are four examples listed in the text?
flashcards.back: There are 15 Flagship Programs. Four examples are the integrated high-speed train network; the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA); the African passport and free movement of people; and “Silencing the guns by 2020.”
flashcards.explanation: The textbook presents these as entries in its list of 15 Flagship Programs intended to support continental growth and transformation.
flashcards.unitTitle: Major Economic and Cultural Activities of Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Africa’s Agenda 2063 and Its Implications
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: When were the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set up, what is their target year, how many goals exist, and under what UN resolution are they contained?
flashcards.back: The 17 SDGs were set up in 2015 by the UN General Assembly, are intended to be achieved by 2030, and are included in a UN Resolution called Agenda 2030.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook describes the SDGs as the post-2015 global development framework succeeding the Millennium Development Goals.
flashcards.unitTitle: Major Economic and Cultural Activities of Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Africa’s Agenda 2063 Vis-A-Vis Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What does the Religious Diversity Index (RDI) measure, and which two African countries score 7.5?
flashcards.back: The RDI uses the population shares of eight major world-religion groups on a 0–10 scale; 10 represents the maximum diversity if all eight groups have equal shares. Guinea-Bissau and Togo each score 7.5.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook describes the index and its scale on printed p. 141, then reports the two 7.5 scores on p. 142. It gives conflicting category labels across those pages, so the card reports scores without assigning either label.
flashcards.unitTitle: Major Economic and Cultural Activities of Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Linguistic and Religious Diversity in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Which sub-region of Sub-Saharan Africa experienced the lowest annual population growth rate (1.8% per year) between 1980 and 2015?
flashcards.back: The Southern sub-region of Africa.
flashcards.explanation: Between 1980 and 2015, Eastern Africa grew at 2.9%, Central Africa at 3.0%, and Western Africa at 2.7%, while Southern Africa had the lower rate of 1.8% per year.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of Global Population Change
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Which two continents together accounted for approximately 77% of the total global human population in 2021?
flashcards.back: Asia (59.5%) and Africa (17.2%).
flashcards.explanation: The cited text says Asia (about 4.68 billion) and Africa (about 1.37 billion) were the only two continents to exceed one billion people and together represented about 77% of the global population.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Overview of Global Population Change
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Which four indirect ecosystem services does the textbook list as supporting economic activity?
flashcards.back: Carbon sequestration, water purification, flood-risk management, and nutrient cycling.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook says the natural environment supports economic growth indirectly through ecosystem services, as well as directly through raw materials such as water, timber, and minerals.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Human–Environment Relationship
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What are three major ways humans modify the physical environment to fulfill their resource needs?
flashcards.back: 1. Cutting down forests to create agricultural land and grow crops; 2. Constructing dams to store water for hydroelectricity, irrigation, and flood control; 3. Drilling into the ground to extract oil and other natural resources.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook gives these as examples of direct human modification of the physical environment to obtain land, energy, water, and other resources.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Human–Environment Relationship
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is planned adaptation to environmental change, and how does it differ from autonomous adaptation?
flashcards.back: Planned adaptation results from a deliberate policy decision based on awareness that conditions have changed or are about to change. Autonomous adaptation is an unplanned response triggered naturally by ecological changes or by market/lifestyle shifts.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook distinguishes a conscious, deliberate policy response from an unplanned response that arises without conscious policy action.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Human–Environment Relationship
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How has indigenous knowledge about biodiversity and natural-resource conservation traditionally been preserved and passed down in Africa?
flashcards.back: It has been accumulated among indigenous peoples and transferred orally across many generations.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook describes African communities as holding extensive knowledge about local plants and environmental systems and transmitting that knowledge orally from generation to generation.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Indigenous Knowledge in Conservation of Natural Resources in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Why did the Teso community strictly prohibit activities such as farming, grazing, and settlement in sacred forest sites?
flashcards.back: The Teso believed spirits would attack anyone who disturbed the peace of the dead. No human activity was allowed at the protected sites where remains were preserved; the sites became dense forest habitats for varied flora and fauna.
flashcards.explanation: The case study links spiritual beliefs to protected areas: prohibiting farming, grazing and settlement allowed vegetation to grow into dense forest that provided habitat for many organisms.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Indigenous Knowledge in Conservation of Natural Resources in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Why did the Teso community protect animals such as snakes, frogs, and toads found in ponds, rivers, and wells from harm?
flashcards.back: They believed these animals helped maintain or sustain the life of important water points.
flashcards.explanation: The cited page says the animals were believed to help sustain important water points; it also identifies rivers and wells as sources of water for livestock and people and as a source of fish.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Indigenous Knowledge in Conservation of Natural Resources in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is "urban primacy" in the context of African urbanization?
flashcards.back: Urban primacy occurs when a single city—usually the capital—possesses a population, economic activity, and political power that are several times greater than those of the next largest city in the country.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook defines urban primacy as a dominant city, usually the capital, whose population, economic activity, and political power are several times greater than those of the next largest city.
flashcards.unitTitle: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Unplanned Urbanization
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What underlying historical, policy, and institutional factors have driven unplanned urbanization in Africa?
flashcards.back: Unplanned and unregulated growth, the legacy of colonialism, policy pressure from international institutions (such as IMF structural adjustment programs), neoliberal policies, and weak urban planning institutions.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook lists unplanned and unregulated growth, colonial legacy, policy pressure from international institutions (including the IMF structural adjustment program), pressure from developed countries through neoliberal policies, and weak urban planning institutions.
flashcards.unitTitle: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Unplanned Urbanization
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: According to the case study of Addis Ababa, what proportion of the population lives in slums, and how are squatter settlements defined?
flashcards.back: More than two-thirds of Addis Ababa's population are believed to be living in slums. The source describes squatter settlements as settlements illegally built, especially on urban-periphery open space, farmland, steep slopes, river buffers, or roadsides, without legal title deeds.
flashcards.explanation: The case study says more than two-thirds of the city’s population are believed to live in slums; it describes the second type of informal settlement as illegal construction on the listed peripheral sites without legal title deeds.
flashcards.unitTitle: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Unplanned Urbanization
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How does the textbook distinguish between voluntary migration and forced migration?
flashcards.back: Voluntary migration is undertaken by choice in search of better economic opportunities or a better quality of life. Forced migration occurs when people are compelled to move to avoid threats such as war, drought, famine, natural disasters, or political conflicts.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook says voluntary migration is generally undertaken in search of better economic opportunities or a good life; forced migration involves people expelled by factors such as war, drought, famine, natural disasters, or political conflicts.
flashcards.unitTitle: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Migration — Factors and Impacts on Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What fundamental structural mismatch creates economic push factors of migration in African places of origin?
flashcards.back: A mismatch between rapid population growth and available resources, together with a low level of requisite technology and limited capacity to create employment at the place of origin.
flashcards.explanation: The passage introduces poor socio-economic conditions, low wages, unemployment, and poverty as economic push factors, then says these are usually brought about by rapid population growth relative to available resources, low requisite technology, and limited employment-creation capacity.
flashcards.unitTitle: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Migration — Factors and Impacts on Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What specific pull factors attract migrants to destination locations?
flashcards.back: Real or perceived opportunities for a better life, higher income, greater physical security, superior quality of education, and better healthcare facilities at the destination.
flashcards.explanation: The source lists real or perceived better-life opportunities, higher income, greater security, and better education and health care at destinations as factors influencing the decision to migrate.
flashcards.unitTitle: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Migration — Factors and Impacts on Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What critical ecological function do wetlands and mangroves perform for coastal waters, and what happens when they are destroyed?
flashcards.back: Wetlands and mangroves act as natural filters for sediment, excessive nitrogen, and wastes. Their destruction accelerates nutrient buildup and coastal water pollution.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook identifies wetlands and mangroves as natural filters for sediment, excessive nitrogen, and wastes; it says their destruction has accelerated nutrient buildup in coastal waters.
flashcards.unitTitle: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Coastal Pollution in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: In the South Africa plastic-pollution case study, what percentage of marine pollution originates from land, how much plastic is recycled, and what happens to the discarded plastic?
flashcards.back: Over 80% of marine pollution in South Africa originates from land-based sources. Sixteen percent of plastic is recycled; the textbook states the rest—about 8 million metric tons of discarded plastic—ends up in rivers and eventually the ocean.
flashcards.explanation: The case study reports South Africa’s 2010 rank of 11th among ocean plastic-pollution offenders and links discarded plastic to wind, littering, improper waste management, and overflowing landfills before it reaches rivers and the ocean.
flashcards.unitTitle: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
flashcards.sectionTitle: Coastal Pollution in Africa
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How does the textbook distinguish between "discrete objects" and "continuous data" in geographic data visualization?
flashcards.back: Discrete objects are features with well-defined, known boundaries in open space (for example, a lake). Continuous data—also called field, non-discrete, or surface data—describes phenomena that progressively vary across a surface or location, with values that may vary from point to point (for example, elevation or temperature).
flashcards.explanation: The source contrasts features with known boundaries, such as a lake, with measurements that vary across a surface, such as elevation.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Basic Concepts of Geospatial Information
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is the fundamental difference between directly collected geographic data and remotely sensed geographic data?
flashcards.back: Directly collected data are generated at the physical source of the phenomenon (e.g., weather station temperature readings, ground survey measurements, tree counts). Remotely sensed data are gathered from a distance without physical contact or visiting the location (e.g., satellite images, aerial photographs).
flashcards.explanation: Direct data collection relies on physical presence or localized instruments on the ground, whereas remote sensing gathers information from airborne or spaceborne platforms.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Sources and Tools of Geographic Data
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is a digitizer, and what does "georeferencing" mean?
flashcards.back: A digitizer is a tool used to convert analogue/paper images into a computer-readable digital format. Georeferencing means relating the internal coordinate system of a scanned map or image to the actual geographic coordinate system of the real-world area.
flashcards.explanation: Digitization converts analogue images into computer-readable form; georeferencing relates the internal coordinate system of a map or aerial photograph to the geographic coordinate system of the area.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Sources and Tools of Geographic Data
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What are the three basic feature types used to define real-world geography on maps, and what is an example of each?
flashcards.back: 1. Point feature: associated with a single location in space (e.g., water well, telephone tower, weather station). 2. Line feature: described by a string of spatial coordinates (e.g., river, road, pipeline). 3. Area (polygon) feature: described by a closed string of spatial coordinates (e.g., forest stand, administrative boundary).
flashcards.explanation: Every geographic object on Earth's surface can be modeled as a point, a linear feature, or an area/polygon.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Geographic Data Representations
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: How does the raster spatial data model structure geographic space and represent points, lines, and areas?
flashcards.back: The raster model uses a grid-cell data structure divided into cells by rows and columns. It represents points as a single cell, lines as a sequence of neighboring cells, and areas as collections of contiguous cells.
flashcards.explanation: The textbook describes raster data as a grid-cell structure with rows and columns; cell size depends on accuracy and resolution, and cells are classified by their most common attribute.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Geographic Data Representations
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: Which key technical advances since the 18th century contributed to accurate modern mapmaking?
flashcards.back: The textbook names advances in mathematics and astronomy, lines of longitude and latitude, improved printing and photography, mass production and accurate reproduction, and the availability of airplanes and satellites. Satellites continuously scan to provide detailed, up-to-date maps of nearly the entire Earth.
flashcards.explanation: The source links modern map accuracy to mathematical and astronomical coordinates, improved reproduction, aerial imagery, and satellite scanning.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Advances in Mapmaking and the Birth of Geographic Information System
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What essential marginal information must be included when finalizing a map layout in GIS (such as ArcMap)?
flashcards.back: Legend, scale bar, north arrow, coordinate information, gridlines, and date of map compilation.
flashcards.explanation: These are the six marginal items the textbook explicitly lists for a completed map layout.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Advances in Mapmaking and the Birth of Geographic Information System
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education

flashcards.front: What is the structural difference between a bar graph and a line graph regarding the data they present?
flashcards.back: A bar graph shows relationships between independent data series where bar height or length represents measured values or frequencies (e.g., monthly rainfall). A line graph shows how connected data changes over time to demonstrate trends (e.g., annual temperature variations).
flashcards.explanation: The textbook defines a bar graph for independent data series and a line graph for how data change over time, especially to show trends or connected numbers.
flashcards.sectionTitle: Making and Interpretation of Graphs, Charts and Diagrams
flashcards.sourcePublisher: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Ministry of Education
